A crew alias points at the core alias by name, so it follows whatever that alias means at resolution time, including a user override; a regression test pins that.
 - **Named project modes.** `mode` is one of `guarded` (default), `pr-only` or `local-only`, with `mergeAutonomy` as a separate opt-in. It derives `github.allowPush` / `github.allowMerge`, applied only where the raw config did not set them explicitly, so an explicit value still wins and every existing enforcement point picks the mode up unchanged. `mode` and `mergeAutonomy` are unreachable from an untrusted project `.model-gateway.json` (the sanitiser is an allowlist).

Under `guarded` it now defaults to `false` unless `mergeAutonomy` is set. Push behaviour is unchanged. Set `"mergeAutonomy": true` to restore the old behaviour.
 - **Scout task shape.** `shape: "ship" | "scout"` on `delegate`, `supervise` and `run_plan` tasks. A scout has its capabilities forced to `read` regardless of what was requested, and reports that it changed nothing — a read-only investigation with an obvious name instead of a hand-written capability list.

label: clean
hunk:
diff --git a/AGENT-INSTALL.md b/AGENT-INSTALL.md
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..185b847
--- /dev/null
+++ b/AGENT-INSTALL.md
@@ -0,0 +1,186 @@
+# Installing Break Free — instructions for a coding agent
+
+You are a coding agent installing **Break Free** on your user's machine. Follow this file top to
+bottom. It is written for you, not for a human: every step says what to run, what a good result
+looks like, and what to do when it is not good.
+
+Break Free is an MCP server plus skills and slash commands that let the agent your user is
+talking to (you) delegate execution to cheaper models, with verification the gateway runs itself.
+Source: <https://github.com/maruthiprithivi/break-free>
+
+## Rules for you
+
+1. **Never put an API key in your transcript, in a file you write, or in a command line.** Keys
+   reach the installer through the user's environment or through the installer's own hidden
+   prompt. If you need a key, ask the user to `export` it themselves and tell you when it is done.
+2. **Never run any of this with `sudo`.** Everything installs under the user's home directory.
+3. **Do not invent answers.** Where a step says to ask the user, ask, and wait.
+4. Report progress as you go, and finish with the report in [Step 6](#step-6-report-back).
+5. If a step fails, stop and read [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) before retrying. Do not
+   re-run a failing command unchanged.
+
+## Step 1: check the prerequisites
+
+```bash
+node -v          # must be v20 or newer
+git --version    # any recent version
+gh auth status   # optional: only needed for the github worker capability
+```
+
+- **Node is missing or older than 20** — stop. Tell the user, and suggest `nvm install 20 && nvm use 20`,
+  or `brew install node` on macOS. Do not try to install Node yourself unless they ask.
+- **git is missing** — stop and tell the user.
+- **`gh` missing or not authenticated** — fine. Continue, and mention in your report that the
+  `github` capability will be unavailable until they run `gh auth login`.
+
+Also check which agent harness is present, because the installer registers itself per harness:
+
+```bash
+command -v claude; command -v codex
+```
+
+At least one must exist. If neither does, stop and tell the user to install
+[Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) or [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) first.
+
+## Step 2: get the source
+
+```bash
+git clone https://github.com/maruthiprithivi/break-free.git ~/.break-free 2>/dev/null \
+  || git -C ~/.break-free pull --ff-only
+cd ~/.break-free
+```
+
+`~/.break-free` is the same location the one-line installer uses, so this stays consistent with
+`curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/maruthiprithivi/break-free/main/install.sh | bash`.
+
+## Step 3: ask the user the four things you cannot decide
+
+Ask all four in one message, then wait for the answers.
+
+1. **Which models should the crew use?** List the options and ask which they have keys for:
+   `deepseek`, `kimi` (Moonshot), `zai` (GLM), `minimax`, `openrouter`, `opencode`,
+   `ollama` (local, no key), `ollama-cloud`, `vllm` (local, no key).
+   *A local Ollama needs no key and no account — a good answer if they have none.*
+2. **Where should it install?** `user` (available in every project — the usual answer),
+   `project` (this repository only), or `both`.
+3. **May delegated workers push to git and merge pull requests?** Default to **no** for both
+   unless they say otherwise. Protected branches default to `main,master,production,release`.
+4. **Do they want GitHub work tracking** (the `break-free-github-flow` skill: an issue per task,
+   CI watching)? `full` adds a standing rule, `skill` installs the commands only, `none` skips it.
+
+Then, for each cloud provider they named, tell them to export the key **in their own shell** and
+confirm when done:
+
+```bash
+export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=...      # MOONSHOT_API_KEY, ZAI_API_KEY, MINIMAX_API_KEY,
+                                 # OPENROUTER_API_KEY, OPENCODE_API_KEY, OLLAMA_API_KEY
+```
+
+You will not see these values, and you do not need to.
+
+## Step 4: install
+
+Write an answers file from what they told you. **Every key field is the literal string `env`** —
+that tells the installer to read the environment variable and store a `${VAR}` reference rather
+than the secret itself. Adjust the provider list, scopes and policy to match their answers:
+
+```bash
+cat > /tmp/break-free-answers.json <<'JSON'
+{
+  "providers": ["deepseek", "ollama"],
+  "claude_scope": "user",
+  "codex_scope": "user",
+  "key_storage": "env",
+  "deepseek_api_key": "env",
+  "ollama_base_url": "http://localhost:11434/v1",
+  "ollama_enabled": true,
+  "protected_branches": "main,master,production,release",
+  "allow_push": false,
+  "allow_merge": false,
+  "github_flow": "skill",
+  "harness_profiles": false,
+  "extra_agents": "detected"
+}
+JSON
+
+node setup.mjs --yes --answers /tmp/break-free-answers.json
+rm -f /tmp/break-free-answers.json
+```
+
+Notes that matter:
+
+- `key_storage: "env"` means the user must export those variables in the shell that launches
+  Claude Code or Codex, not only in the shell that ran the installer. Say this in your report.
+- `"providers"` limits the run to the providers named. Anything omitted is left untouched.
+- Omit `"project_dir"` unless a scope is `project` or `both`; then set it to the repository path.
+- Set `"harness_profiles": true` only if the user wants to run Claude Code or Codex *on* one of
+  these models. It is unrelated to delegation and off by default here.
+- The installer is safe to re-run. It merges into any existing config and keeps a `.bak` of every
+  file it rewrites.
+
+Read the output. The last line is the verdict:
+
+| Verdict | Meaning | What you do |
+|---|---|---|
+| `GREEN` | everything checked out | continue to Step 5 |
+| `GREEN with warnings` | usable; something optional is missing | continue, and list the warnings in your report |
+| `RED` (exit 1) | something must be fixed | stop, read the `FAIL` lines — each carries its own `fix:` — and see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) |
+
+## Step 5: verify it actually works
+
+Do not take the installer's word for it. Run these and read the output:
+
+```bash
+node ~/.break-free/setup.mjs --doctor     # expect: no FAIL lines
+claude mcp list                           # expect: break-free-gateway ... Connected
+```
+
+For Codex, check that `~/.codex/config.toml` now contains an `[mcp_servers.break_free_gateway]`
+table.
+
+Then confirm a model actually answers. From inside the user's agent session:
+
+```
+list providers
+```
+
+A table of usable providers means the install is live. If you can call MCP tools directly, call
+`list_providers` with `probe: true` and then `test_provider` with `spec: "<provider>"`; the latter
+reports latency, the reply, and whether tool-calling works.
+
+## Step 6: report back
+
+Give the user exactly this, filled in:
+
+- **Verdict** from the installer, and any warnings.
+- **Installed**: which harnesses were registered, at which scope.
+- **Providers**: which verified, with the default model each resolved to.
+- **Environment variables they must keep exported**, and in which shell.
+- **What is not available yet** (for example: `github` capability until `gh auth login`).
+- **What to try first**, verbatim:
+  ```
+  /break-free-resume
+  /break-free-delegate fast write unit tests for <a real file in their project>
+  ```
+- **Uninstall**, if they want it gone: `node ~/.break-free/setup.mjs --uninstall` (add `--purge`
+  to also delete config, keys and sessions).
+
+## Troubleshooting
+
+| What you see | Cause | What to do |
+|---|---|---|
+| `Node ... is too old` | Node below 20 | Stop. `nvm install 20 && nvm use 20`, then re-run Step 4. |
+| Installer ends `RED` | a preflight or postflight check failed | Read the `FAIL` line; it carries its own `fix:`. Then `node setup.mjs --doctor`. |
+| A provider fails verification | wrong key, or a model that no longer exists | Confirm the variable is exported **in this shell** (`printenv DEEPSEEK_API_KEY | wc -c`, never print the value). The installer offers another model or another key. |
+| `claude mcp list` shows it but not connected | the build did not run, or the path moved | `node ~/.break-free/setup.mjs --yes` rebuilds and re-registers. |
+| Codex refuses to start, mentions `wire_api` | a leftover `wire_api = "chat"` provider | `node setup.mjs --doctor` finds it and offers to rewrite it. |
+| Everything fails and you suspect the installer | — | `bash ~/.break-free/setup/selftest.sh` tests the installer in isolation against fake CLIs and a mock provider. |
+| A worker misbehaves later | — | `node setup.mjs --doctor` reads the runtime log and names the failing provider, or run the `gateway_logs` tool. |
+
+## Do not
+
+- Do not commit the answers file, or any file containing a key, to any repository.
+- Do not set `allow_push` or `allow_merge` to `true` without the user explicitly asking.
+- Do not remove `protected_branches`.
+- Do not install with `sudo`, and do not write outside the user's home directory.
+- Do not report success on a `RED` verdict.

+## Routing "use X to do Y"
+
+When the user says "write code using deepseek", "use codex for the mockups", "use kiro-cli and agy to review" — route by what `X` is, a **model** or a **harness**:
+
+| "X" | route | example |
+|---|---|---|
+| a model/provider spec (`deepseek`, `kimi`, `zai`/`glm`, `minimax`, `ollama`, `openrouter/…`, `opencode/…`) | **LLM delegation** — `delegate`/`run_plan` with `model` | "write code using deepseek" → `delegate {model:"deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro", task:"…"}` |

+| several harnesses | one `harness_spawn` per harness, send each the same task, read each back | "use kiro-cli and agy to review" → spawn both, send the diff + "review this" to each, `harness_read` both |
+

 ### Added
 
+- **Browser extension: DLP enforcement is now observable from outside the
+  extension (#1791).** Every egress decision on the paste and send paths
+  carries a four-state verdict -- `blocked`, `warned`, `allowed`,
+  `not_evaluated` -- in a new additive `enforcement` field on the audit row,
+  alongside `rule_state`, `decision_origin` and, for a non-evaluation, a named
+  `not_evaluated_reason`. The backend persists all four into the audit Tags
+  map (no schema change, no migration).

+  This closes a gap that survived the first #1791 fix. A clean paste on a
+  fully-protected device previously produced NO audit row -- and so did a
+  device where the extension was switched off for the site, where the user had
+  paused it, or where the content script never evaluated anything. From the
+  audit trail, "we scanned this and it was clean" and "we never scanned
+  anything" were the same observation: silence. `allow` is the audit decision
+  verb for both, which is why `decision` alone could not carry the difference.
+
+  Concretely, three branches that were bare `return`s now record their own
+  named reason (`dlp_not_evaluated_site_disabled`, `dlp_not_evaluated_paused`,
+  `dlp_not_evaluated_unknown_verdict`), and a scanned-and-clean egress emits a
+  `dlp_enforced_clean` proof-of-enforcement row. One state is explicitly NOT
+  observable and says so in the code: when the extension context is
+  invalidated, `chrome.runtime` is gone and no row can be sent -- the external
+  signal there is the service-worker heartbeat stopping.
+
+  **Who is affected:** anyone consuming the browser audit stream sees new rows
+  and new tag keys. Nothing is removed and no existing row changes shape.
+  Volume is bounded: the `allowed` and `not_evaluated` rows are sampled once
+  per (egress origin, reason) per content-script session, a declared property
+  of the vocabulary rather than an implementation detail. Blocked and warned
+  rows remain per-event, unchanged.
+
+- **Browser extension: the heartbeat now reports enforcement posture (#1791).**
+  Every 5-minute heartbeat carries `rule_state`, `enforcing` and
+  `rules_loaded`, persisted into the heartbeat audit row's Tags.
+
+  Until now the only evidence that a device was not enforcing came from an
+  egress ATTEMPT -- someone had to paste or send. A device whose rule sync had
+  been failing since install, on which nobody pasted that day, emitted
+  heartbeats byte-identical to a fully-armed one: `total_matches_session: 0`
+  means both "saw nothing sensitive" and "cannot see anything at all". An
+  admin can now answer "which devices are installed and NOT enforcing" from
+  the fleet record, with no user action and without trusting the extension's
+  own popup.

+  degraded, not disarmed, and saying otherwise would tell an admin they are
+  unprotected when they are not. A device on an older build reports no posture
+  at all, and the backend records that as ABSENT rather than as `false`:
+  "this build does not report its posture" and "this device is not enforcing"
+  are different facts.

@@ -41,8 +42,57 @@ jobs:

+        with:
+          fetch-depth: 0
+
+      # Decide whether this PR touches the enforcement path. On merge_group the
+      # answer is always "no": relevance was already decided at PR time and the
+      # job passes by construction, matching regression-gate.yml.
+      #
+      # The verdict is PRINTED either way. "not applicable" and "ran and found
+      # nothing" must never look the same -- that is the distinction this whole
+      # epic is about, and a silent skip would reintroduce it in the gate built
+      # to prevent it.
+      - name: Does this PR touch the enforcement path?
+        id: rel
+        env:
+          BASE_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
+          HEAD_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
+        run: |
+          set -euo pipefail
+          # push-to-main still carries a paths filter, so arriving here at all
+          # means enforcement files changed -- run. Skipping here would mean the
+          # guard NEVER runs on main, which is where a bad merge actually lands.
+          if [ "${{ github.event_name }}" = "push" ]; then
+            echo "relevant=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
+            echo "APPLICABLE: push to main matched the enforcement paths filter."
+            exit 0

+          # merge_group: relevance was decided at PR time; pass by construction,
+          # matching regression-gate.yml.
+          if [ "${{ github.event_name }}" != "pull_request" ]; then
+            echo "relevant=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
+            echo "NOT APPLICABLE: ${{ github.event_name }} -- relevance was decided at PR time."
+            exit 0
+          fi
+          CHANGED="$(git diff --name-only "$BASE_SHA...$HEAD_SHA")"
+          if [ -z "$CHANGED" ]; then
+            echo "::error::could not compute the changed-file list; refusing to "\
+                 "report NOT APPLICABLE on an empty diff, which would pass this "\
+                 "gate for every PR."
+            exit 1
+          fi
+          if echo "$CHANGED" | grep -qE '^(sdks/python/controlzero/controlzero/_internal/enforcer\.py|sdks/python/controlzero/controlzero/client\.py|scripts/ci/mutation-guard\.py|scripts/ci/skip-budget\.(py|json)|sdks/python/controlzero/tests/|\.github/workflows/mutation-guard\.yml)'; then

+            echo "APPLICABLE: this PR touches the enforcement path; running the full guard."
+          else
+            echo "relevant=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
+            echo "NOT APPLICABLE: no enforcement-path files changed in this PR."

task: docs(claude): a control with two halves needs a test for the seam (#2370) (#2373)
label: clean
hunk:
diff --git a/CLAUDE.md b/CLAUDE.md
index fe8106b1d..8d083ea31 100644
--- a/CLAUDE.md
+++ b/CLAUDE.md
@@ -898,3 +898,66 @@ skipping to green because CI never sets the DSN), #1927/#1931 (these).
 **When you add or touch a gate, ask: if this silently stopped working, what
 would look different? If the answer is "nothing", that is the defect -- fix that
 first.**
+
+## A control with two halves needs a test for the SEAM (ABSOLUTE, post-2026-08-17, #2370)
+
+On the PUBLISHED wheel 1.13.13, editing a signed policy file flipped a `deny`
+into an `allow` and `guard()` silently obeyed. The `.sig` sidecar was sitting
+right there, no longer matching, and nothing read it.
+
+Both halves were tested, correctly, by properly driven tests:
+
+- `test_tamper.py:76` writes a genuinely mutated envelope to a real file and
+  proves `load_signed_file` rejects it. **Detection: proven.**
+- `test_tamper_behavior.py:66` proves `guard()` fails closed -- by passing
+  `context={"tamper_detected": True}`. **Response: proven. The CALLER asserts
+  the very fact the control exists to discover.**
+
+Nothing connected them. Every test in both files passed the entire time.
+
+This is #2340 one step harder, and the difference is what makes it a rule.
+There, a test asserted a case the system never produces -- findable by reading
+that one test, whose own comment stated the defect. Here both tests are
+individually above reproach and the defect is **the absence of a third test
+nobody wrote.** A reviewer opening either file finds nothing wrong. Absence is
+the harder review problem, and it is the one to design against.
+
+### Rules
+
+1. **Any control with a DETECT step and a RESPOND step needs a test that drives
+   the real trigger through the public entry point and asserts the response.**
+   Not detection alone. Not response alone. The two are typically written at
+   different times, by different people, in different files, and each half will
+   report healthy forever while the wire between them is cut.
+2. **Ask of every control: what test fails if the wiring is cut?** If the answer
+   is "none", that is a live hole, not a coverage gap.
+3. **A test that HANDS the control the fact it exists to discover is proving the
+   response, not the control.** Grep for this shape and treat each hit as
+   unproven until a driven test exists:
+   `context={"tamper_detected": True}`, `decision=PolicyDecision(...)`,
+   `SomeGuard._private_helper(...)`. The #2356 audit classified 10 documented
+   behaviours **6 DRIVEN / 4 FABRICATED** using exactly that question.
+4. **Enumerate the TYPES and FORMS real callers pass, and parametrise on them.**
+   The first fix for #2370 stored the policy path only when it was already a
+   `Path`:
+
+   ```python
+   self._local_policy_path = local_source if isinstance(local_source, Path) else None
+   ```
+
+   `Client(policy="policy.yaml")` -- a string -- is what every documentation
+   example uses, so verification was skipped for essentially every real caller,
+   while the new test, which builds a `Path`, went green. **A control present,
+   tested, and unreachable, inside the fix for a control that was present,
+   tested, and unwired.** An `isinstance` narrowing is a silent capability gate.
+   The regression test is parametrised on the ARGUMENT TYPE; that is the thing
+   that makes the hole impossible to reintroduce.
+5. **A subagent reporting "N passed" is telling you its test is green. It is
+   never evidence the product works.** Re-derive the claim yourself through the
+   public entry point, in the form a customer uses. That single step is what
+   caught rule 4, on a fix whose own test suite was passing.
+6. **Marketing and blog claims get executed too, not just docs.** Before
+   publishing a post claiming a deny rule blocks `rm -rf ~/`, we ran it against
+   the published wheel: three deny cases and two allow cases, all correct. That
+   check costs minutes and is the only thing separating a true claim from
+   #2340.

+# BYOK unit economics and the LLM-proxy commercial model: external evidence

+
+This document answers six questions about the commercial model for the Control Zero
+LLM-proxy gateway using published external sources only. Every factual claim carries
+a source URL. Where a number could not be verified, the document says so explicitly
+rather than substituting a plausible figure.
+
+Two framing notes, both load-bearing:
+
+1. **I was not shown the founder's draft pricing document.** The final section responds
+   to the pricing parameters as stated in the research brief -- a "Tier 2" BYOK tier, a
+   6% top-up fee, a $10 minimum top-up, payload logging at 100M requests/month, and
+   Stripe Billing Meters as the billing mechanism. If the draft says something different
+   from those parameters, the contradictions listed there need re-checking against it.
+2. **Prices move.** Everything below was fetched on 2026-08-08. Vendor pricing pages
+   change without notice and several of these vendors have changed their fee structure
+   within the last 18 months (OpenRouter twice). Re-verify before anything is committed

+from the stack (Postgres only, no ClickHouse proposal appears below); Doppler is

+Workers) -- note that Vercel still appears below purely as a _competitor_ whose gateway

+[Braintrust pricing](https://www.braintrust.dev/pricing), [Vercel AI Gateway pricing](https://vercel.com/docs/ai-gateway/pricing).
+
+### Additional comparables found while searching
+
+Not in the brief's list, but they matter because they establish where the market is
+converging on BYOK:
+
+- **Pydantic AI Gateway**: "Bring your own provider credentials (BYOK): free on every
+  plan, no markup. Built-in providers: 5% markup on Personal and Team, 3% on Growth."
+  ([source](https://pydantic.dev/ai-gateway))
+- **LLM Gateway (llmgateway.io)**: "The only platform fee is a flat 5% when you buy
+  credits." BYOK: "No platform fee. With your own provider keys (BYOK), routing through

+  retention, stored requests are billed at **$0.01 per 1M tokens**."
+  ([source](https://llmgateway.io/pricing))
+- **LangSmith LLM Gateway**: in public beta, included with LangSmith Plus and Enterprise
+  plans; supports BYO API key or Gateway Credits. GA pricing not yet published.
+  ([source](https://www.langchain.com/langsmith/llm-gateway))
+
+### Goldly
+
+goldly.ai returns effectively nothing to a text fetch (a single header line: "GOLDLY AI
+GROUP -- Global AI Infrastructure & Intelligent Applications"). The only substantive
+public document located is a corporate deck hosted on a third-party site
+([PDF](https://wrc.cie.org.cn/profile/robot/download/2026/07/31/20260731234459000004_20260731234459A101.pdf)).
+
+From that deck, GOLDLYAI Group describes three business pillars: AI-Infra (multi-cloud
+GPU/CPU compute), **AI-Gateway (a global LLM API gateway)**, and AI-Agent. The gateway
+pillar runs three aggregation platforms: _Shengsheng Token_ (tokenshengsheng.com,
+consumer, described in the deck as "benchmarked against OpenRouter", claiming 100,000+
+users), _Wenwen Token_ (tokenwenwen.com, enterprise, "40+ providers, 99.9% uptime"), and
+_PandasRouter_ (pandasrouter.com, Chinese models -- Qwen, Kimi, DeepSeek, GLM -- billed

+**No pricing, fee percentage, or BYOK terms are published.** Goldly is positioning
+evidence (a competitor explicitly benchmarking itself against OpenRouter, with a
+China-model routing angle we do not have), not pricing evidence. Do not cite it as a
+pricing comparable.
+
+### The pattern that matters
+
+Of the seven products in the brief's list, **exactly one charges a fee for BYOK, and it
+has publicly stated its intention to stop.** Portkey, Helicone, LiteLLM, Cloudflare and
+Vercel all support BYOK at no percentage fee; Pydantic and LLM Gateway explicitly market
+BYOK-is-free as a differentiator. Vercel states it flatly: "With BYOK, there is no markup
+or fee from AI Gateway."
+
+The revenue models that work in this set do not tax BYOK inference. They charge for
+either (a) the convenience of consolidated billing when the customer uses _the vendor's_
+credentials, or (b) the platform's own storage and processing -- logs, traces, scores,
+retention -- which is a real cost the vendor incurs.

+## B. OpenRouter's BYOK fee, precisely
+
+This is the closest published precedent to a Tier 2 BYOK fee, so it is worth getting
+exactly right.
+
+**The fee: 5% of what the same model and provider would normally cost on OpenRouter,
+deducted from the customer's OpenRouter credit balance -- not from their own provider
+account.** It is charged in addition to what the customer's own provider key is already
+being billed.
+
+> "Yes, if you choose to use your own provider API keys (Bring Your Own Key - BYOK), the
+> first 1M BYOK requests per-month are free, and for all subsequent usage there is a fee
+> of 5% of what the same model and provider would normally cost on OpenRouter. This fee
+> is deducted from your OpenRouter credits."
+> -- [OpenRouter FAQ](https://openrouter.ai/docs/faq)
+
+Corroborated by their support article: "OpenRouter charges a 5% platform fee on the
+provider's cost for requests you make with your own key -- but only after you pass a
+monthly allowance. The first 1,000,000 BYOK requests each calendar month are free of
+this fee... the counter resets at the start of the next month (UTC)."
+([source](https://openrouter.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/43219817892123-Why-Am-I-Still-Being-Charged-When-Using-My-Own-Key-BYOK))
+
+History: BYOK launched at 5% in December 2024 ("BYOK is available for 5% of the upstream
+provider's cost", [announcement](https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/bring-your-own-api-keys/)).
+The 1M free requests/month allowance was added 1 October 2025
+([announcement](https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/1-million-free-byok-requests-per-month/)).
+
+### Three findings that change how this precedent should be read
+
+**1. OpenRouter's own published materials state the free threshold two different ways,
+and they are not equivalent.**
+
+- The FAQ and BYOK docs say: **1,000,000 BYOK requests per month.**
+- The pricing page says, under "BYOK Limits": Pay-as-you-go gets **"$25,000 of list price
+  inference / month with no fees, 5% fee after"**; Enterprise gets **"$200,000 of list
+  price inference / month with no fees, 5% fee after."**
+  ([source](https://openrouter.ai/pricing))
+
+A request count and a dollar-of-list-price threshold are different units and will bind at
+completely different points for any given customer. I could not determine from public
+sources which one is actually enforced, or whether the pricing page reflects a newer
+tiering that the FAQ has not caught up with. **Do not model Tier 2 off "1M requests" as
+though it were settled -- the market leader's own docs disagree with themselves.** If this
+precedent is going to anchor our pricing, it is worth an email to OpenRouter support to
+establish which is real.
+
+Also note that the BYOK docs page at `/docs/use-cases/byok` currently renders its fee as
+unexpanded template variables (`{openRouterBYOKFee.fraction}%`, waived for the first
+`{BYOK_FEE_MONTHLY_REQUEST_THRESHOLD}` requests) -- the literal numbers come from the FAQ,
+the support article, the pricing page and the announcements, which is why all four are
+cited above rather than one.
+
+**2. OpenRouter has publicly said it intends to remove the percentage BYOK fee.**
+
+> "BYOK fee: The current 5% usage-based fee will be removed in the future and replaced
+> with a fixed monthly subscription (pricing TBD -- suggestions welcome!)"
+> -- [Simplifying Our Platform Fee, 9 June 2025](https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/simplifying-our-platform-fee/)
+
+That was 14 months ago and the 5% fee is still live, so this is a stated intention rather
+than a completed change. But the direction is unambiguous, and it is the direction the
+rest of the market is already at: **the one company charging a percentage on BYOK has
+announced it wants to be charging a flat subscription instead.** Building Tier 2 as a
+percentage-of-BYOK-inference fee means adopting a model its only practitioner has
+publicly disowned.
+
+**3. The fee has a documented support burden.**
+
+OpenRouter maintains a dedicated support article titled "Why Am I Still Being Charged
+When Using My Own Key (BYOK)?" The article explains that unexpected charges have two
+common causes -- automatic provider fallback silently using OpenRouter's shared capacity
+instead of the customer's key, and the 5% platform fee -- and walks the customer through
+distinguishing them in the Activity page. A fee structure that requires a troubleshooting
+article to explain why "bring your own key" still produces a bill is a customer-trust
+cost, not just a pricing line.
+
+Related and relevant to how we would have to build it: OpenRouter's budgets and spend
+controls "count only OpenRouter credit spend by default", so BYOK inference does not
+count toward a customer's configured budget unless they explicitly enable
+`include_byok_in_budgets`. Their own blog flags this: "if your team runs mostly on its own
+provider keys, a budget covers less of the bill than it looks like it does."
+([source](https://openrouter.ai/blog/insights/governing-team-ai-spend/)) If we sell spend
+governance, a BYOK path that silently escapes the budget control is the exact
+failure-looks-like-success shape our own engineering rules forbid.
+

+## C. Observed cost structure of AI coding agents at scale
+
+### From the Databricks post
+
+[Managing AI Coding Costs at Scale](https://www.databricks.com/blog/managing-ai-coding-costs-scale),
+published 2026-08-07 by Patrick Wendell, Akshat Bhatia, Vinay Gaba, Erich Elsen and Ivan
+Zhou, with acknowledged review from infrastructure leaders at Uber, Stripe, Coinbase and
+Ramp.
+
+The post is deliberately light on absolute numbers. It contains exactly two quantified
+claims:
+
+- **Routing:** "Internal results at Databricks suggest that our AI Gateway Smart Router is
+  able to consistently reduce average task cost by more than 30%, while roughly matching
+  the quality of the most expensive model in the working set."
+- **Token overhead and caching:** "At Databricks, relatively simple tuning of our harness
+  and caching settings led to an almost 50% reduction in the number of generated tokens
+  and associated costs, with no observed quality degradation for developers."
+
+It publishes no cost per developer per month, no cache hit rates, no request volumes, and
+no developer counts. The savings table is an image and its per-technique figures are not
+in the page text; the post itself describes those numbers as "directional, based on an
+informal survey of development teams."
+
+What the post is actually useful for is **the shape of the demand we would be selling
+into**, which is directly relevant to positioning:
+
+- It names the category we are building in and defines it: "AI Gateway" -- a central
+  location doing (1) capacity management and proxying, (2) budget tracking and
+  enforcement including "progressive friction levels and model downshifting", (3)
+  configuration management for end-user tools to "enforce model allow-lists, compaction
+  settings", and (4) "logging of coding session traces for downstream efficiency analysis".
+- **It explicitly rejects hard budget caps as the primary control.** "Hard budgets, where
+  usage is entirely cut off at a specific spend threshold, are often used only as a last
+  resort option in every company we spoke with", for two stated reasons: cutting off a
+  developer is "debilitating to productivity", and high spenders are often the highest-
+  output users. The recommended pattern is visibility, then self-clearing spend gates,
+  then approval-gated spend gates, then **downshifting to a cheaper model**, with
+  suspension only in the limit case.
+- Two named evaluation results where a newer, more expensive model was rejected: "Stripe
+  found that Opus 4.7 did not meaningfully improve quality over Opus 4.6, while increasing
+  cost. They therefore declined to make Opus 4.7 available internally. Databricks saw
+  similar cost regressions when comparing Opus 5.0 to 4.8."
+- The strategic argument: chase the "efficiency frontier" (best price for a given
+  intelligence level), not the intelligence frontier, because the efficiency frontier
+  "is advancing far faster."
+
+Note that Databricks has open-sourced or made free its gateway (Unity AI Gateway) and
+meta-harness (Omnigent), and states "Thousands of companies use these components every
+day." That is a free competitor in the cost-control-gateway category, from a vendor with
+distribution. It does not do what we do on policy/DLP/audit, but it does budgets,
+routing, proxying and trace logging for free.
+
+### Real per-developer numbers from other sources
+
+The Databricks post does not provide these, so they come from elsewhere.
+
+**First-party, from Anthropic's own documentation** (the strongest source in this
+section):
+
+> "Across enterprise deployments, the average cost is around $13 per developer per active
+> day and $150-250 per developer per month, with costs remaining below $30 per active day
+> for 90% of users."
+> -- [Manage costs effectively, docs.claude.com](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/costs)
+
+**Measured usage data, 792 developers**, from Viberank's
+[State of AI Coding Spend 2026](https://www.viberank.app/blog/state-of-ai-coding-2026)
+(published 2026-06-10; developers run `ccusage` against their own local agent logs and
+submit). 2.5T tokens, $2.3M of API-equivalent usage value, 29,230 coding days:
+
+- Daily burn: **median day $29, p90 day $215, p99 day $708**. Largest single day recorded:
+  $3,820. 11% of all tracked days exceeded $200.
+- Lifetime value per developer: p25 $379, median $1,285, p75 $3,128, p90 $6,494, p99
+  $30,720. Top user: $56,694 across 81 billion tokens.
+- Power law: "The top 1% of users account for 14% of all spend. The top 10% account for
+  51%. The top 25% account for 74%."
+- Normalized monthly: "roughly half run at $1,000+/month in API-equivalent value, and ~73%
+  run above $400/month. Most of them pay $100-200/month flat for Claude Max."
+
+Their own stated caveats are important and I am repeating them rather than laundering the
+numbers: submissions are self-selected onto a usage leaderboard and therefore skew heavy
+("Read these numbers as benchmarks for serious users, not population averages"); "spend"
+means API-equivalent list value, not out-of-pocket; and coverage skews to Claude Code.
+
+**Survey data:** Gartner Peer Insights research reports 23% of tech leaders spending
+$200-500 per developer per month on tokens for AI coding agents, and 6% of organisations
+paying more than $2,000 per developer per month
+([Computer Weekly](https://www.computerweekly.com/news/366645054/Gartner-AI-coding-agents-will-cost-more-than-real-developers)).
+
+**Reported enterprise reaction:** Uber capped employee spend at $1,500/month per AI coding
+tool after exhausting its full-year 2026 agentic coding budget in roughly four months; a
+Microsoft division reportedly moved engineers off Claude Code onto flat-rate Copilot after
+token billing reached ~$2,000/engineer/month
+([particula.tech analysis](https://particula.tech/blog/ai-coding-agent-cost-per-engineer-spend-caps),
+[morphllm summary](https://www.morphllm.com/ai-coding-costs)). These are secondary sources
+reporting on press coverage; treat as directional, not verified.
+
+### The cache-hit economics -- the most important number in this section
+
+From the Viberank dataset, the token mix across all 2.5 trillion tracked tokens:
+
+| Token class      | Share     |
+| ---------------- | --------- |
+| Cache reads      | **94.8%** |
+| Cache writes     | 4.2%      |
+| Input (uncached) | 0.8%      |
+| Output           | **0.2%**  |
+
+> "For every token an agent actually writes, it re-reads ~406 tokens of cached context...
+> This is why prompt caching, not model price, is the real economic engine of agentic
+> coding."
+
+This single fact drives three conclusions that bear directly on our model:
+
+1. **Any pricing metric based on tokens is dominated by cache reads**, which are the
+   cheapest token class (Anthropic prices cache reads at 10% of the input price). A
+   percentage-of-token-spend fee and a percentage-of-request-count fee will diverge
+   enormously for the same workload.
+2. **Cache-aware routing is a first-class cost lever, and cache-blind routing destroys
+   value.** Databricks makes the same point independently: "Routing for agentic use cases
+   also needs to account for server-side caching, since a cold cache hit has a very high
+   cost for large context workloads." A proxy that breaks or fails to preserve prompt
+   caching can make a customer's bill worse, not better. That is a product risk, not just
+   a pricing one.
+3. **Payload logging cost is driven by the 94.8%, not the 0.2%.** See section E.
+

+## D. Is 6% competitive, and what does it actually net at $10?
+
+Two separate questions. The answers point in opposite directions, which is the trap.
+
+### Is 6% competitive? No -- it would be the highest published fee in the category.
+
+| Vendor                | Published platform/top-up fee                                                   |
+| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
+| Vercel AI Gateway     | **0%** (no markup, no platform fee; payment processing fees passed to customer) |
+| Pydantic AI Gateway   | 3% (Growth) / 5% (Personal, Team) on built-in providers; **0% on BYOK**         |
+| Cloudflare AI Gateway | 5% on Unified Billing credits                                                   |
+| LLM Gateway           | 5% on credit purchases                                                          |
+| OpenRouter (crypto)   | 5.0% flat, no minimum                                                           |
+| OpenRouter (card)     | **5.5%, $0.80 minimum**                                                         |
+| **Proposed**          | **6%**                                                                          |
+
+6% is above every published comparable. It is above the highest (OpenRouter's 5.5%) and
+6 percentage points above the most aggressive (Vercel's zero). Note also that Portkey,
+Helicone, LiteLLM and Braintrust do not charge a percentage at all -- they charge
+subscription plus metered logs/data, so for those vendors the comparable fee is
+structurally 0% and the money comes from somewhere else entirely.
+
+### Does 6% cover Stripe at the $10 minimum? Barely, and not at all internationally.
+
+Stripe's published standard rates ([stripe.com/pricing](https://stripe.com/pricing)):
+
+- **2.9% + $0.30** per successful transaction, domestic cards
+- **+1.5%** for international cards
+- **+1%** if currency conversion is required
+- **$15.00** dispute received fee, plus $15.00 dispute countered fee (refunded only if you
+  win)
+
+Modelling a customer paying $X and receiving $X minus the fee in credit:
+
+| Top-up | Stripe cost (domestic) | Effective Stripe rate | 6% revenue | **Net margin** | Margin as % of top-up |
+| ------ | ---------------------- | --------------------- | ---------- | -------------- | --------------------- |
+| $10    | $0.59                  | 5.90%                 | $0.60      | **$0.01**      | 0.1%                  |
+| $25    | $1.03                  | 4.10%                 | $1.50      | $0.47          | 1.9%                  |
+| $50    | $1.75                  | 3.50%                 | $3.00      | $1.25          | 2.5%                  |
+| $100   | $3.20                  | 3.20%                 | $6.00      | $2.80          | 2.8%                  |
+
+**At the $10 minimum, a 6% fee nets one cent.**
+
+With an international card (+1.5%, so 4.4% + $0.30):
+
+| Top-up | Stripe cost | 6% revenue | **Net margin**    |
+| ------ | ----------- | ---------- | ----------------- |
+| $10    | $0.74       | $0.60      | **-$0.14 (loss)** |
+| $25    | $1.40       | $1.50      | $0.10             |
+| $50    | $2.50       | $3.00      | $0.50             |
+
+With an international card requiring currency conversion (+1.5% +1%, so 5.4% + $0.30):
+
+| Top-up | Stripe cost | 6% revenue | **Net margin**                 |
+| ------ | ----------- | ---------- | ------------------------------ |
+| $10    | $0.84       | $0.60      | **-$0.24 (loss)**              |
+| $25    | $1.65       | $1.50      | **-$0.15 (loss)**              |
+| $50    | $3.00       | $3.00      | **$0.00 (exactly break-even)** |
+
+**Break-even top-up size for a flat 6% fee:**
+
+- Domestic card: **$9.68**
+- International card: **$18.75**
+- International card + currency conversion: **exactly $50.00**
+
+So yes -- **flag confirmed: 6% is under water at small top-ups.** A $10 minimum sits 32
+cents above the domestic break-even and well below the international one. Given Control
+Zero's customer base includes non-US organisations (active APAC proof-of-concept work,
+the EU/APAC surface), a material share of top-ups will be international cards, and every
+$10 and $25 international top-up loses money.
+
+Dispute economics make it worse. A single $15 dispute-received fee wipes out the margin on
+**1,500 domestic $10 top-ups**. Two disputes (received + countered, if lost) wipe out
+3,000. Small prepaid balances bought on cards are a chargeback-prone product shape.
+
+### What OpenRouter did, and why
+
+OpenRouter's fee is 5.5% _with a $0.80 minimum_ -- and they published the before/after
+table when they introduced it:
+
+| Order size | Old fee | New fee         |
+| ---------- | ------- | --------------- |
+| $5         | $0.61   | **$0.80 (16%)** |
+| $10        | $0.88   | **$0.80 (8%)**  |
+| $25        | $1.67   | $1.38           |
+| $100       | $5.61   | $5.50           |
+| $1,000     | $52.98  | $55.00          |
+
+([Simplifying Our Platform Fee](https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/simplifying-our-platform-fee/))
+
+They deliberately made small top-ups _proportionally expensive_ -- 16% on a $5 order -- and
+large ones cheaper. The $0.80 minimum exists precisely to cover Stripe's fixed $0.30
+component plus margin. At a $10 top-up, OpenRouter nets $0.80 - $0.59 = **$0.21, which is
+21 times the one cent a flat 6% yields.** They also removed a previously separate fixed
+$0.35 Stripe fee in the same change, folding it into the minimum.
+
+The structural lesson: **a flat percentage cannot price a transaction that has a fixed
+cost component.** Any percentage low enough to be competitive is below cost at small
+amounts, and any percentage high enough to cover $0.30 at $10 is uncompetitively high at
+$1,000. The fix is not a different percentage -- it is a percentage plus a floor.
+
+For reference, to net $0.20 on a $10 domestic top-up requires a fee of $0.79. That is
+within a cent of OpenRouter's $0.80. Two independent derivations landing on the same
+number is reasonable evidence the number is right.
+
+### One structural note on Stripe Billing Meters
+
+Stripe Billing Meters bill usage in arrears against a subscription. A prepaid credit
+top-up is a different money flow -- a one-off PaymentIntent that increments a balance we
+hold. **A "top-up fee" only exists if there are top-ups, which means a credit balance,
+which means a ledger.** Project memory records a founder decision that billing is Stripe
+Meters and that the prepaid wallet/reservation model was dropped. If that decision stands,
+a 6% top-up fee has nothing to attach to; if top-ups are back, then the wallet is back and
+that decision needs revisiting explicitly rather than by implication. **This needs
+resolving before any of the arithmetic above matters.** I have flagged it rather than
+assumed a resolution because I was not shown the current draft.
+

+## E. Payload logging at 100M requests/month
+
+### What comparable products actually do
+
+Every product examined does at least one of: separate payload from metadata, meter logs
+independently of requests, cap or truncate, or default payloads off.
+
+| Product                   | Payload logging behaviour                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
+| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
+| **OpenRouter**            | **Off by default.** "Prompt and completion are not logged by default. We do zero logging of your prompts/completions, even if an error occurs, unless you opt-in." Opt-in is incentivised with **a 1% discount on usage costs** -- they pay customers for payloads rather than charging them ([FAQ](https://openrouter.ai/docs/faq))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
+| **Cloudflare AI Gateway** | On by default, but **payload storage is separable from the log entry**: the `cf-aig-collect-log-payload` header controls raw request/response bodies independently of `cf-aig-collect-log`, so "metadata such as token counts, model, provider, status code, cost, and duration will still be logged". Hard caps: **10 MB per log (logs larger are not stored)**, 500 logs/sec/gateway ingest, **10 million logs per gateway** (paid), 100,000 total (free), with configurable auto-delete-oldest ([logging](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/observability/logging/), [limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/reference/limits/)) |
+| **Portkey**               | **Meters recorded logs, not requests**, and degrades logging rather than traffic: "Exceeding this limit doesn't affect your requests; only logs beyond the limit are not recorded." Retention 3 days (free) / 30 days (Production) ([pricing](https://portkey.ai/pricing))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
+| **LLM Gateway**           | **Metadata free; full payloads priced separately at $0.01 per 1M tokens**, retention 30 days free tier ([pricing](https://llmgateway.io/pricing))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
+| **Braintrust**            | Charges directly for **processed data: $4/GB (Starter), $3/GB (Pro)**; retention 14/30 days included, then **$0.50/GB/month** ([pricing](https://www.braintrust.dev/pricing))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
+| **Helicone**              | 1 GB storage free; retention tiered 7 days / 1 month / 3 months / forever; **ingest rate-limited by plan** at 10 / 1,000 / 15,000 / 30,000 logs per minute ([pricing](https://www.helicone.ai/pricing))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
+
+**The single most useful data point:** Cloudflare -- a company whose entire business is
+operating storage and network at planetary scale -- caps AI Gateway at **10 million logs
+per gateway**. The brief's scenario is 100M requests/month, which is **ten times
+Cloudflare's per-gateway ceiling**, and they still make customers choose between
+auto-deleting the oldest and stopping new logs. Nobody in this comparison set offers
+unbounded full-payload retention at that volume at a flat price, because it is not a
+flat-price-shaped cost.
+
+The market answer to "what do they do" is therefore, consistently: **metadata always,
+payloads opt-in or separately priced, hard size cap per log, aggressive retention
+expiry, and logging degrades before traffic does.**
+
+### Volume math
+
+Payload sizes for coding agents are large because, per section C, 94.8% of tokens are
+cache reads -- the model is re-reading a large context on nearly every turn, and that
+context is in the request body. Logging full payloads on an agentic workload means
+persisting that re-read context over and over.
+
+I do not have a verified first-party figure for average agent payload size. One secondary
+source (a developer blog, [dev.to](https://dev.to/gabrielanhaia/llm-trace-storage-cost-why-your-s3-bill-exploded-and-3-fixes-4880),
+cited as illustrative not authoritative) reports "A single span on a long agent turn runs
+80 KB. A 47-turn agent run hits 4 MB", and that at 200 req/s "the payload bytes outweigh
+the span metadata roughly 50 to 1." Cloudflare's 10 MB per-log cap is an independent
+signal that individual payloads do reach the multi-megabyte range.
+
+At 100M requests/month, with the average combined request+response payload as the
+variable:
+
+| Avg payload | Monthly volume | 12-month accumulation |
+| ----------- | -------------- | --------------------- |
+| 5 KB        | 0.5 TB/mo      | 6 TB                  |
+| 10 KB       | 1 TB/mo        | 12 TB                 |
+| 50 KB       | 5 TB/mo        | 60 TB                 |
+| 100 KB      | 10 TB/mo       | 120 TB                |
+
+These are arithmetic, not measurements. **Before any storage design is committed,
+instrument the real p50/p95/p99 payload size on actual traffic.** Designing this off an
+assumed average is exactly the failure mode our own engineering rules call out --
+establish state by driving the code, not by reading a declaration.
+
+### Storage economics, with the Postgres-only constraint
+
+**Verified price anchor.** Cloudflare R2 ([pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing/)):
+
+- Standard storage: **$0.015 / GB-month**; Infrequent Access: $0.01 / GB-month
+- **Class A operations (writes, `PutObject`): $4.50 / million**
+- Class B operations (reads, `GetObject`): $0.36 / million
+- Egress: free; free tier 10 GB-month, 1M Class A, 10M Class B
+
+At 100M payloads/month written as objects:
+
+- Write operations alone: 100M x $4.50/M = **$450/month**, before storing a single byte
+- Storage at 5 TB/month accrual: $75/month for month one, rising to ~$900/month by month
+  twelve if nothing expires
+
+The operations cost exceeds the storage cost by roughly 6x in month one. **At this
+volume, the cost driver is the per-object write, not the gigabyte.** That conclusion
+generalises: any design that does one durable write per request pays a per-request price,
+and 100M/month is a large multiplier on any per-request price.
+
+**Postgres specifically.** I could not obtain a vendor-published $/GB for managed
+Postgres storage (see "What I could NOT verify"). But the disk price is not the binding
+constraint, and treating it as one would be the wrong analysis. The binding constraints
+at 100M payload rows/month in Postgres are:
+
+- **Row count.** 100M rows/month is 1.2B rows/year in one table. This requires
+  partitioning (monthly or weekly) from day one -- retrofitting partitioning onto a
+  1B-row table in production is a migration we would not want to run.
+- **TOAST.** Postgres stores values above roughly 2 KB out-of-line in a TOAST side table,
+  compressed. Every payload at any of the sizes modelled above exceeds that threshold, so
+  each logged payload is at minimum an extra out-of-line write plus its own index entry.
+  Payload logging in Postgres is not "a wide column", it is a second table with its own
+  bloat and vacuum characteristics.
+- **Write amplification and WAL.** Every insert is written to the WAL and then to the
+  heap. 5 TB/month of payload becomes at least 10 TB/month of write I/O, and all of it
+  flows to every replica and into every base backup. Backup size, restore time and
+  replication lag all scale with payload volume, not with request count.
+- **Autovacuum.** A high-churn, high-volume table with an aggressive retention policy
+  generates dead tuples at the rate of the retention deletions. `DELETE` at this scale is
+  substantially worse than `DROP PARTITION`, which is another reason partitioning is
+  mandatory rather than optional.
+- **Blast radius.** This table shares an instance with the operational database that
+  serves policy decisions. A logging-volume incident becomes an enforcement-path incident.
+  Given the enforcement product is the thing customers trust us with, coupling the audit
+  payload store to the decision path in the same Postgres instance is a risk that needs
+  an explicit decision, not a default.
+
+**Recommendation shape** (not a decision, and it respects the Postgres-only constraint
+because it does not propose a second _database_): keep metadata in Postgres, where it
+belongs -- it is small, structured, queryable, joins to orgs and policies, and is what
+almost every product surface actually reads. Put payloads in object storage keyed by the
+metadata row id, with a per-log size cap and a retention policy, and make payload capture
+an explicit per-org/per-rule setting that defaults conservative. This is precisely
+Cloudflare's split (`cf-aig-collect-log` vs `cf-aig-collect-log-payload`) and LLM
+Gateway's split (metadata free, payloads priced), arrived at independently by both.
+
+Two constraints that follow directly from our own engineering rules and should be written
+into whatever design lands:
+
+- **"Not logged" must be distinguishable from "logged and empty."** A payload that was
+  never captured, one that was captured and truncated, one dropped because it exceeded the
+  size cap, and one that genuinely had no content are four different states. An empty
+  payload field standing for all four is the silent-success shape we have been bitten by
+  repeatedly.
+- **Logging must degrade before traffic does.** Portkey states this explicitly as product
+  behaviour. If the payload store is unavailable, the request must still be evaluated and
+  served, and the audit record must record that the payload was unavailable -- not
+  silently omit it.
+
+---
+
+## F. BYOK legal and ToS risk
+
+**This is the section with a genuine go/no-go finding in it.** I am not a lawyer and this
+is not legal advice; what follows is what the contracts say, quoted, with the ambiguities
+flagged rather than resolved.
+
+The question: do Anthropic, OpenAI and Google's terms permit a third party to proxy a
+customer's own API key?
+
+### OpenAI: an explicit clause that squarely names the activity
+
+[OpenAI Services Agreement](https://openai.com/policies/services-agreement/), section 3.3
+Restrictions:
+
+> "Customer will not, and will not permit End Users to: ... **(g) buy, sell, or transfer
+> API keys from, to, or with a third party**"
+
+And section 3.1, Customer Account:
+
+> "Customer will not share Account access credentials or individual login credentials
+> between multiple users. **Customer may not resell or lease access to its Account or any
+> End User Account.**"
+
+This is the sharpest clause across all three providers. Two readings are available and
+they lead to different answers:
+
+- **Narrow reading:** 3.3(g) targets a _market_ in API keys -- buying, selling and
+  trafficking them as commodities. A customer configuring a vendor to act as their agent,
+  using their key on their behalf and at their direction, is agency, not transfer. On this
+  reading BYOK is fine, and the fact that OpenAI's own ecosystem is full of BYOK gateways
+  (Vercel, Cloudflare, OpenRouter, Portkey, Pydantic all offer OpenAI BYOK, OpenRouter
+  since December 2024) supports it.
+- **Broad reading:** "transfer API keys ... to a third party" is not qualified by
+  consideration. Uploading a secret key into another company's system so it can
+  authenticate as you is, literally, transferring the key to a third party. Section 3.1's
+  prohibition on sharing credentials "between multiple users" points the same way.
+
+I could not find any OpenAI guidance, FAQ, or enforcement action resolving which reading
+OpenAI applies. **The widespread market practice is evidence about enforcement
+likelihood, not about contractual permission** -- and our own engineering rules are
+explicit that we do not assert an external vendor's behaviour from inference. This one
+needs counsel, and if the answer matters commercially it needs it before Tier 2 ships,
+not after.
+
+### Anthropic: no equivalent clause found; a resale restriction that could bite
+
+[Anthropic Commercial Terms of Service](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms).
+I read the full document. **There is no clause prohibiting a customer from providing their
+API key to a third-party processor.** The relevant provisions:
+
+- **A.1 Overview** is permissive: "Anthropic gives Customer permission to use the
+  Services, including to power products and services Customer makes available to its own
+  customers and end users ('Users')."
+- **D.4 Use Restrictions:** "Customer may not and must not attempt to (a) access the
+  Services to build a competing product or service, including to train competing AI models
+  or **resell the Services except as expressly approved by Anthropic**; (b) reverse
+  engineer or duplicate the Services; or (c) support any third party's attempt at any of
+  the conduct restricted in this sentence."
+- **D.5 Service Account:** "Customer is responsible for all activity under its account."
+- **D.2** incorporates the Usage Policy, Supported Regions Policy and Service Specific
+  Terms by reference. I did not read those three documents in this pass; **if this
+  question goes to counsel, they should be included in scope** -- an API-key clause could
+  live in the Service Specific Terms and I have not ruled that out.
+
+The risk for Anthropic is not the customer's BYOK -- it is **our own Tier 1**. D.4's
+resale restriction ("resell the Services except as expressly approved by Anthropic")
+applies to a model where we buy inference on our own Anthropic key and sell it on to
+customers as credits. That is the _non_-BYOK path, and it is the path a credit/top-up
+model implies. Note that the "except as expressly approved" wording means approval is
+obtainable -- this is a conversation to have with Anthropic, not a wall.
+
+D.5 also cuts our way as a reason customers _want_ BYOK: the customer remains responsible
+for all activity on their account, which is an argument for giving them a gateway that
+enforces their policy on that activity.
+
+### Google: credential confidentiality plus a sublicensing prohibition
+
+Gemini API is governed by two stacked documents. The
+[Gemini API Additional Terms](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms) (effective 2026-03-23)
+open by requiring acceptance of both: "you must accept (1) the Google APIs Terms of
+Service (the 'API Terms'), and (2) these Gemini API Additional Terms of Service."
+
+The operative clauses are in the base
+[Google APIs Terms of Service](https://developers.google.com/terms/) (last modified
+2021-11-09):
+
+Section 4(b)(1), Confidential Matters:
+
+> "**Developer credentials (such as passwords, keys, and client IDs) are intended to be
+> used by you and identify your API Client. You will keep your credentials confidential
+> and make reasonable efforts to prevent and discourage other API Clients from using your
+> credentials.** Developer credentials may not be embedded in open source projects."
+
+Section 4(a)(1), API Prohibitions:
+
+> "When using the APIs, you may not (or allow those acting on your behalf to): 1.
+> **Sublicense an API for use by a third party.** Consequently, you will not create an API
+> Client that functions substantially the same as the APIs and offer it for use by third
+> parties."
+
+Section 2(c), Permitted Access, adds: "You will not misrepresent or mask either your
+identity or your API Client's identity when using the APIs."
+
+Google's is the most awkward wording for a BYOK gateway. "Intended to be used by you and
+identify your API Client", combined with an obligation to "prevent and discourage **other
+API Clients** from using your credentials", describes a hosted proxy authenticating with
+the customer's key fairly precisely -- our gateway is a different API Client using their
+credentials. The counter-argument is that a gateway operating under the customer's
+direction is part of _their_ API Client rather than another one, and Google's ToS
+predates the AI-gateway category by several years (last modified November 2021). Again:
+unresolved, needs counsel.
+
+Section 4(a)(1)'s sublicensing prohibition is a Tier 1 concern for the same reason
+Anthropic's D.4 is: reselling access on our own key.
+
+### Summary of F, and what to do about it
+
+| Provider      | Explicit key-sharing restriction?                                                                                                           | Resale/sublicense restriction?                                 | Risk to Tier 2 (customer BYOK)   | Risk to Tier 1 (our key, resold)               |
+| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
+| **OpenAI**    | **Yes** -- 3.3(g) "buy, sell, or transfer API keys from, to, or with a third party"; 3.1 no credential sharing, no reselling account access | Yes (3.1)                                                      | **Highest. Direct textual hit.** | High                                           |
+| **Anthropic** | **None found** in Commercial Terms (Usage Policy and Service Specific Terms not reviewed)                                                   | Yes -- D.4, resale "except as expressly approved by Anthropic" | Low on the text as read          | Moderate, and approval is expressly obtainable |
+| **Google**    | **Partial** -- credentials "intended to be used by you", must "prevent and discourage other API Clients from using your credentials"        | Yes -- 4(a)(1) no sublicensing                                 | Moderate                         | Moderate                                       |
+
+**The brief is right that this is a real risk nobody has checked, and it is not
+symmetrical across providers.** The single highest-risk item is OpenAI 3.3(g), because it
+names API key transfer explicitly rather than requiring interpretation of a general
+clause.
+
+What I would want before shipping Tier 2, in order of cost:
+
+1. **Read the three documents I did not read**: Anthropic's Usage Policy and Service
+   Specific Terms, and OpenAI's usage policies. Cheap, and could change the table above.
+2. **Counsel review of OpenAI 3.3(g) specifically**, with the narrow/broad readings above
+   as the question. This is the go/no-go.
+3. **Ask the providers directly.** Anthropic's D.4 says resale is permitted "as expressly
+   approved" -- so ask. A written answer from each provider is worth more than any amount
+   of inference from what competitors get away with, and it is the only thing that
+   converts this from an assumed risk into a known one.
+4. **Design-level mitigations that are worth doing regardless of the legal answer**:
+   customer keys encrypted at rest with per-org keys and never logged; the customer, not
+   us, remains the contracting party with the provider; no fallback from the customer's
+   key to our key without explicit opt-in (OpenRouter's silent fallback is the subject of
+   their most-read support article, and doing it silently would also misattribute spend);
+   and a documented ability for the customer to revoke.
+
+One further note relevant to how we would market this. Cloudflare's BYOK documentation
+makes a point worth copying: BYOK "changes which credential authenticates the upstream
+request -- it doesn't change which endpoints you're allowed to route to", and a BYOK key
+"does not exempt a provider from your Zero Data Retention or `data_collection`
+restrictions" ([OpenRouter BYOK docs](https://openrouter.ai/docs/use-cases/byok) make the
+same point). Customers will assume BYOK means their data policy is satisfied. It does
+not, and saying so plainly is both accurate and a differentiator for a governance product.
+
+---
+
+## What this changes about the proposed model
+
+Responding to the pricing parameters as stated in the research brief. I did not see the
+founder's draft document; each item below names the parameter it contradicts so it can be
+checked against the real draft.
+
+### 1. A percentage fee on BYOK inference is the wrong instrument -- and its only practitioner is abandoning it
+
+**Contradicted:** Tier 2 as a percentage fee on BYOK, with OpenRouter cited as precedent.
+
+OpenRouter is not a precedent for a growing practice; it is the last one doing it. Six of
+the seven products in the comparison charge nothing for BYOK, two of them market
+BYOK-is-free as a differentiator, and OpenRouter itself announced in June 2025 that the 5%
+usage fee "will be removed in the future and replaced with a fixed monthly subscription."
+Adopting a percentage BYOK fee in August 2026 means adopting the model the category has
+already moved away from, at a moment when our differentiator (policy, DLP, audit,
+enforcement) is something none of the free-BYOK vendors sell.
+
+**What the evidence supports instead:** charge for the governance product per seat or per
+org, and let BYOK inference pass through at zero. We are not an inference reseller; the
+value we add is not proportional to the customer's token spend, and pricing it as though
+it were invites the customer to route around us at exactly the volumes where our controls
+matter most.
+
+### 2. 6% is simultaneously the highest fee in the market and below cost at the minimum
+
+**Contradicted:** the 6% figure and the $10 minimum, together.
+
+These two numbers fail in opposite directions at once, which is the tell that the
+instrument is wrong rather than the number:
+
+- Against competitors, 6% is the highest published fee in the category (versus 5.5%
+  OpenRouter, 5% Cloudflare and LLM Gateway, 3-5% Pydantic, 0% Vercel).
+- Against Stripe, 6% nets **$0.01** on a domestic $10 top-up, **loses $0.14** on an
+  international $10 top-up, and **loses $0.24** on an international card requiring
+  currency conversion. Break-even is $9.68 domestic, $18.75 international, and exactly
+  $50.00 international-with-conversion.
+
+**Fix, and it is the one OpenRouter already converged on:** a lower percentage with a
+fixed minimum. A ~5% fee with a ~$0.80 floor covers Stripe's fixed $0.30 at every top-up
+size, nets ~$0.21 on a $10 top-up rather than $0.01, and prices below the highest
+competitor rather than above it. Deriving the floor from our own margin target on a $10
+domestic top-up gives $0.79, within a cent of OpenRouter's published $0.80.
+
+Also raise the minimum top-up. A $10 minimum on international cards is a loss-maker under
+any percentage low enough to be competitive; $20-25 is the smallest defensible floor, and
+disputes ($15 each way) argue for higher still.
+
+### 3. A top-up fee presupposes a credit ledger that was already decided against
+
+**Contradicted:** a "top-up fee" coexisting with "Stripe Billing Meters" as the billing
+mechanism.
+
+Billing Meters bill metered usage in arrears against a subscription. A top-up is a prepaid
+balance -- a one-off payment incrementing a ledger we maintain. Project memory records a
+founder decision that billing is Stripe Meters and the prepaid wallet/reservation model
+was **dropped**. If that decision stands, there are no top-ups to charge 6% of, and
+section D's arithmetic is moot. If top-ups are back, the wallet is back, and that reversal
+should be made explicitly with its costs (ledger, reconciliation, refund policy, unused
+balance liability, revenue recognition) rather than arriving as a side effect of a pricing
+line. **This is the first thing to resolve; several other items depend on it.**
+
+### 4. Payload logging at 100M requests/month is a per-write cost, not a storage cost, and 100M is 10x the market's ceiling
+
+**Contradicted:** payload logging at 100M requests/month treated as a flat included feature.
+
+Cloudflare caps AI Gateway at 10 million logs per gateway and 10 MB per log, and still
+makes customers choose between auto-deleting oldest and dropping new logs. The brief's
+volume is ten times that ceiling. No comparable offers unbounded full-payload retention at
+this volume at a flat price.
+
+The cost shape is also the opposite of the intuitive one: at 100M writes/month, R2's Class
+A operations alone are **$450/month before storing a byte**, roughly 6x the first month's
+storage cost at a 5 TB accrual. Per-request costs dominate; per-gigabyte costs do not.
+
+**What the evidence supports:** meter logs separately from requests (Portkey), separate
+payload capture from metadata capture as an explicit setting (Cloudflare), price full
+payload retention as its own line if offered at all (LLM Gateway at $0.01/1M tokens,
+Braintrust at $3-4/GB), cap per-log size, and expire by partition. And instrument the real
+payload size distribution before committing -- every number in section E's volume table is
+arithmetic on an assumed average, not a measurement.
+
+### 5. The BYOK ToS question is unresolved and asymmetric, and OpenAI is the sharp edge
+
+**Contradicted:** any plan that treats BYOK as legally uniform across providers.
+
+OpenAI's Services Agreement 3.3(g) prohibits customers from "transfer[ring] API keys
+from, to, or with a third party" -- a clause that names the activity directly rather than
+requiring interpretation. Google requires customers to "prevent and discourage other API
+Clients from using your credentials." Anthropic's Commercial Terms contain no equivalent
+clause.
+
+This does not mean BYOK is prohibited -- there is a credible narrow reading of 3.3(g), and
+the entire market operates on the broad assumption that it is fine. It means **we do not
+know**, the exposure differs by provider, and we would be building a governance product on
+an unexamined contractual assumption. Get counsel on OpenAI 3.3(g), and ask the three
+providers in writing. The cost of asking is a few emails; the cost of being wrong is a
+tier we have to withdraw.
+
+### 6. Two things in the brief's framing that the evidence supports, and should not be cut
+
+Stated because under-claiming is as inaccurate as over-claiming, and both of these
+survived the research:
+
+- **The category is real and the buyer is identified.** Databricks' post defines "AI
+  Gateway" as a named infrastructure category with four functions, three of which we
+  already have, and reports that companies including Stripe, Coinbase, Uber and Ramp are
+  building or buying exactly this. The demand is not speculative.
+- **Cache-aware behaviour is a genuine technical moat, and a genuine risk.** 94.8% of
+  agentic tokens are cache reads. A proxy that preserves prompt caching correctly is
+  worth real money to a customer (Databricks: ~50% token reduction from caching and
+  harness tuning alone); a proxy that breaks it makes their bill worse. This deserves an
+  explicit test in our gateway before we sell on cost control at all -- and it is the kind
+  of control whose failure would look exactly like success from our side, so it needs to
+  be measured against the provider's reported cache-read counts, not against our own
+  emitted metrics.
+
+---
